Around the year 1000, sea trade across the Indian Ocean linked East Africa, Arabia, the Persian Gulf, India, Southeast Asia and China into one connected market. The network was far older and lasted for centuries; this marker shows it at full stretch.

It ran on the monsoon. The winds blow from the north-east in winter and from the south-west in summer, so a ship could sail one way and come back months later when the wind turned. Arab and Persian dhows with planks sewn together with coir rope, Indian and Malay ships, and Chinese junks all used it.

Who traded what:

  • The Swahili city-states sold gold from the interior, later from Great Zimbabwe, with ivory, slaves and timber.
  • Arab and Persian merchants linked the markets of the Abbasid Caliphate and the Fatimid Caliphate to the ocean through ports such as Siraf and Aden.
  • South India under the Chola dynasty sold cotton cloth and pepper, and Chola fleets even raided Southeast Asia.
  • Srivijaya, on Sumatra, controlled the Strait of Malacca and its tolls.
  • China under the Song dynasty sent porcelain and silk, and its merchants sailed further than before.

Along these routes Islam spread down the African coast and across to Southeast Asia, and Indian religions and writing had already shaped Java and Cambodia. Later, Zheng He's fleets crossed the same waters, and after Vasco da Gama reached Calicut in 1498 the Portuguese tried to control the trade by force.
